1.name: Fuel tank
1.spec: Welded, 106 L, in the wing root bay between the spars
1.note: Sits above everything it feeds: its surface stands about 1.36 m over the carburettor, and that height is the system's only pump.

2.name: Filler adapter and cap
2.spec: Riveted adapter ring, locking cap flush with the upper skin
2.note: Seals the top of the tank so that the only way for air to come in is the vent: a cap left loose lets fuel siphon out in flight.

3.name: Finger strainer
3.spec: Ø19 brass mesh tube, 8 mesh, on the outlet
3.note: Keeps debris out of the line. Its lowest slots stand 24 mm above the floor, so water and sediment settle in the sump below it, and the fuel under it is unusable.

4.name: Sump quick-drain valve
4.spec: Spring-closed poppet at the tank's low inboard corner
4.note: Pushed open with a sampler cup before flight: water, being heavier, lies here first and comes out first.

5.name: Quantity sender
5.spec: Float on a 330 mm arm, rheostat on the outboard end wall
5.note: The float rides the surface; its arm turns a rheostat whose resistance the gauge reads as a quantity.

6.name: Vent line
6.spec: Ø9.53 tube from the tank's high end, forward-facing under the wing
6.note: Lets air in as fuel leaves. Facing forward it catches ram air, about +1.5 kPa in cruise; blocked, the tank's ullage turns into a vacuum.

7.name: Vent check valve
7.note: Opens to let air into the tank but closes against fuel trying to leave by the vent, as it would when the tank warms or the aeroplane banks.

8.name: Feed line
8.spec: Ø9.53 × 0.89, tank to selector, down the front door post
8.note: About 2.6 m of 7.75 mm bore. At cruise flow it loses well under a kilopascal: in a gravity system the height matters far more than the pipe.

9.name: Selector valve body
9.spec: Two inlet ports at ±45° from forward, outlet below, cover above
9.note: Under the cabin floor between the seats. Its bore holds the rotor; the two tank lines come in from forward, the outlet leaves downward.

10.name: Selector rotor
10.spec: Ø36 plug with a 120° window and a centre bore
10.note: Its window spans 60° either side of the handle: pointing forward it uncovers both ports (BOTH), pointing aft neither (OFF).

11.name: Rotor O-ring
11.spec: 2-024, above and below the ports' plane
11.note: Seal the rotor in its bore so fuel goes only where the window lets it, not round the plug.

12.name: Detent ball and spring
12.spec: Ø4.8 ball in the cover, into dimples on the rotor's top
12.note: Clicks the rotor into each of the four positions, so the handle cannot be left halfway with both ports half shut.

13.name: Selector shaft and handle
13.spec: Through the floorboard; the handle points at the tank in use
13.note: The handle is the rotor's pointer: wherever it points on the placard, the window faces that way under the floor.

14.name: Line, selector to strainer
14.spec: Ø9.53 × 0.89, forward under the floor and through the firewall
14.note: Carries all the engine's fuel, so the flow, and the friction loss, is twice that of either tank line on BOTH.

15.name: Shut-off valve
15.spec: Push-pull, knob on the panel, cabin side of the firewall
15.note: Cuts the fuel at the firewall, for an engine fire, whatever the selector says.

16.name: Strainer top casting
16.spec: Inlet left, outlet right, primer tapping on top
16.note: Bolted at the firewall's lowest point: fuel comes in, goes down outside the screen into the bowl, then up through the screen and out.

17.name: Strainer bowl
17.note: Wide enough that the fuel crosses it at a few mm/s, slower than a 0.15 mm water drop falls, so water settles to its floor.

18.name: Screen
18.spec: Ø26 cylinder, 100 mesh, closed cap, held up by a spring
18.note: Everything the engine gets passes through it; the coarse dirt the finger strainers let by stops here.

19.name: Bowl gasket
19.spec: Flat ring in the casting's groove
19.note: Seals the bowl to the casting. A leak here would let air in and fuel out at the system's lowest point.

20.name: Bowl retaining nut
20.spec: Threaded collar on the casting's spigot
20.note: Pulls the bowl's lip up against the gasket. Unscrewed, the bowl and screen come off for cleaning.

21.name: Strainer drain valve
21.spec: Spring-closed poppet at the bowl's centre, opened from the cabin
21.note: Pulled before flight until the fuel runs clear: about 20 mL/s flows, water first, because it sits at the bottom.

22.name: Hose to the carburettor
22.spec: Ø9.5 bore, fire-sleeved, strainer to float valve
22.note: Flexible because the engine moves on its mounts; it ends at the float valve's inlet, about 0.85 m above the ground.

23.name: Carburettor
23.spec: Updraft, float type, under the engine
23.note: Its float needle closes the inlet as the bowl fills: it takes exactly what the engine burns, as long as the head can push that much in.

24.name: Primer body
24.spec: Barrel through the panel, valve block with two ports
24.note: A small hand pump on the panel, fed from the strainer's top, piped to the cylinders' intake ports.

25.name: Primer plunger and knob
25.spec: Ø14.3 piston, 45 mm stroke: 7.2 mL a stroke
25.note: Pulled out it draws fuel in; pushed in it sprays it into the intake ports, so a cold engine fires before the carburettor can feed it.

26.name: Primer check balls
26.spec: Ø4.76 balls on their seats, inlet below, outlet above
26.note: One-way valves: the inlet ball lifts on the pull, the outlet ball on the push, so the pump moves fuel one way only.

27.name: Primer lines
27.spec: Ø3.18 tubes, strainer to primer to the intake ports
27.note: Thin because they carry only millilitres; locked with the knob pushed in, so the engine cannot suck fuel through them in flight.

28.name: Fuel quantity gauge
28.spec: Dual, L and R needles, 2 in
28.note: Reads each sender's rheostat. It reads true only in level, unaccelerated flight, which is why pilots also dip the tanks and keep time.
